Sanctions Hit Madagascar Oil & Gas Producers, Sparking Uncertainty for Industry Workers

Antananarivo – The oil and gas sector in Madagascar is facing mounting pressure following new international sanctions targeting its leading producers. The measures, announced last week by a coalition of Western nations, have resulted in an immediate halt to exports from several key extraction sites, including those operated by Malagasy PetroResources and Southern Basin Energy.

Industry representatives reported that shipments from the Ambilobe and Morondava fields have been blocked since Tuesday, with local management describing a “rapidly deteriorating operating environment.” The sanctions, which restrict access to foreign markets and freeze overseas assets of Malagasy oil and gas firms, have already led to the suspension of ongoing expansion works at the Anosy onshore project.

“We are working to maintain essential operations, but the uncertainty is having a real impact on our workforce,” said Jean Rakotomalala, spokesperson for the Madagascar Oil & Gas Producers’ Union. He indicated that at least 300 contract workers had their shifts cancelled this week, with more layoffs feared if the situation persists.

Analysts say the sanctions are expected to significantly curtail output, which could jeopardize the industry’s medium-term investment plans. “This is a shock to a sector that had just begun to recover from previous downturns,” noted Marie Rasoanaivo, an independent energy analyst based in Antananarivo.

Union leaders have called for urgent discussions with government officials to safeguard the interests of thousands of employees across the country. As the situation develops, oil and gas extraction and production activities remain disrupted, with no clear timeline for resolution.
